title: Apple finally fixed Siri. So why does it feel anticlimactic?
summary: Apple's long-delayed AI overhaul finally makes Siri a capable assistant, but the launch feels underwhelming against a landscape of advanced AI agents that can code, reason, and create media. The improvement, while genuine, arrives in a moment when basic AI competence no longer feels revolutionary.
content: Apple’s long-awaited AI overhaul finally makes Siri the assistant it was always supposed to be. But after years of delays, the launch lands in an AI landscape where chatbots have evolved into agents that can code, reason, create media, and complete complex tasks. Siri AI is genuinely useful, yet it arrives at a moment when simply being a capable AI assistant no longer feels revolutionary.

title: Europe’s AI labeling and transparency rules are now in effect
summary: The EU's new AI Act transparency requirements took effect on August 2nd, requiring companies to disclose when people interact with AI and when content is AI-generated or altered. The rules aim to help users identify chatbots and AI deepfakes while varying requirements based on whether companies are AI providers or deployers.
content:
The EU made some AI labels that companies can use instead of designing their own. | Image: The European Commission / The Verge	

The European Union has ushered in some additional rules that aim to make it easier for people to identify chatbots and AI deepfakes online. The new transparency obligations under the bloc's landmark AI Act came into effect on August 2nd, requiring companies to disclose when people are interacting with AI models, and if content has been generated or altered by them.
The transparency rules differ between providers (companies that develop and market AI systems) and deployers (platforms and services that use those AI systems), though some companies like Meta and SpaceXAI are classified as both.

title: The first-gen Kindle Scribe is a big e-reader and digital notebook that’s $150 refurbished
summary: The first-generation Kindle Scribe is available refurbished for $149.99 with a Premium Pen through August 8th, offering a large 10.2-inch screen suitable for textbooks and handwritten notes. Recent software updates added AI-powered note-taking features, making it a practical option for students despite lacking waterproofing.
content:
The Scribe comes with a Premium Pen, which includes a built-in eraser. | Photo by Amelia Holowaty Krales / The Verge	

The Kindle Scribe is worth considering if you’re heading back to school, as its large 10.2-inch screen can display textbooks and ebooks, or let you jot down handwritten notes during class. Now through August 8th, the first-gen model (with a Premium Pen) is down to just $149.99 with 16GB of storage in refurbished condition at Woot when you apply the promo code KINDLE25 at checkout. That’s $220 off its original launch price from 2022 and even cheaper than the current Kindle Paperwhite, though you’ll only get Woot’s 90-day warranty. Woot doesn’t specify the exact condition of its refurbished devices, but it does offer a brief explanation here of what to expect.
Kindle Scribe (16GB)

Where to Buy:

 $369.99 $149.99 at Woot (with code KINDLE25)

The Kindle Scribe features a sharp 300ppi E Ink display that’s glare-free and supports adjustable color temperatures, making it easy to read whether you’re outside in the sun or studying late at night. Like all other Kindles, the Scribe gives you quick and easy access to Amazon’s massive store of digital books, so you can switch between assigned reading and your favorite novels without carrying multiple books or devices. It’s not waterproof like the Kindle Paperwhite, though, so you’ll want to keep it away from the pool and be careful when it rains.
It’s also a solid digital notebook, with the device offering a variety of pre-made templates for everything from lined paper and planners to to-do lists. After updating the software, the original Kindle Scribe also includes the same AI-powered note-taking features as the newer models, allowing you to jot down notes directly on compatible ebook pages, summarize and refine your handwritten notes, generate AI-powered summaries, and more. 
Read our Kindle Scribe (2022) review.

title: Bluesky’s new CEO wants a big tent, not a bubble
summary: Toni Schneider, former CEO of Automattic/WordPress, has taken over as Bluesky's CEO and aims to build an open, interoperable social ecosystem rather than a closed platform. He frames the current moment as similar to the early web, positioning success as a vibrant multi-player ecosystem that could take a decade to develop.
content:
Today, I’m talking with Toni Schneider, who is the brand new CEO of the social platform Bluesky — he formally took over after a short stint as interim CEO.
This is one of my favorite kinds of interviews to do on Decoder, because a couple years ago, we had Bluesky’s prior CEO, Jay Graber, on the show — she’s now the company’s chief innovation officer, and all of that kind of shuffle is pure Decoder bait. And a new CEO often brings with them new priorities, which is perhaps the most Decoder subject of all.
Bluesky in particular is a company pulling in a lot of different directions: There’s a Twitter-like social media app, which is what most people are familiar with, and then there’s the underlying technology behind that app call AT Protocol, which allows anyone to build social networking products that interoperate with Bluesky. As you’ll hear Toni say, that ecosystem is vibrant and growing — it’s called the ATmosphere, which is adorable.
But the users of Bluesky the app are not the same as the people building on AT Protocol, and the goals of a company founded to push forward the ideas of open and interoperable social standards are not necessarily aligned with the things all those users might need or want. This is a fight that bursts into view on Bluesky itself all the time, and I wanted to know how Toni thinks about balancing all of that with what remains a fairly small team.



Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

title: Samsung’s 2TB 9100 Pro SSD is actually somewhat reasonably priced
summary: Samsung's 2TB 9100 Pro SSD is available for $302.99 on Amazon, roughly $100 less than usual. As Samsung's first PCIe Gen 5 drive, it offers double the speeds of its predecessor at a competitive price point for high-capacity storage.
content:
Next to buying RAM, finding a fast, high-capacity NVMe SSD at a reasonable price has been a challenge during RAMageddon. I don’t want to say it’s getting easier, but one of Samsung’s latest SSDs is cheaper than it has sold for since February 2026. That’s something, right? Amazon has the heatsink-less version of the Samsung 9100 Pro with 2TB of storage for $302.99, which is about $100 less than the usual price. Granted, it sold for a low of $169.99 back in October 2025, but it’s a smart purchase right now compared to buying the 1TB model for $250.
Samsung 9100 Pro NVMe SSD

Where to Buy:

 $500 $302.99 at Amazon (2TB, no heatsink)
 $500 $399.99 at Best Buy (2TB no heatsink)

The 9100 Pro is Samsung’s first SSD to support PCIe Gen 5, making it a great fit if you have the right motherboard and other parts to get as much speed from it as possible. Its theoretical maximum random read and write speeds are at least twice as fast as the 990 Pro SSD that it replaced. However, it’s good (albeit slower than advertised) in a PCIe Gen 4 setup, as well. 
It’ll work fine without a heatsink in a PC or laptop (though, it’s never a bad idea to use one that fits in your system). However, you’ll need to install a heatsink in order to use this in a PlayStation 5, due to potential heat issues that could damage the SSD if used without one. Thankfully, heatsinks are super affordable, and come in a range of designs and price points.
Other great Verge-approved deals
Another Samsung-made product made the cut for today’s roundup. Its Smart Monitor lineup is worth considering if you want a PC monitor that can double as a TV, as well as a screen that you can do video chats on. Its 32-inch M8 4K monitor just hits its lowest price at Amazon and B&H Photo, selling for $349.99 — exactly 50 percent off its original $699.99 price that it hasn’t sold for since the turn of the year. title: How headlights got brighter, whiter, and more blinding after dark
summary: Modern vehicle headlights have become brighter and more technically advanced than ever before, though improvements in brightness and color temperature come with increased glare that can blind other drivers.
content: Automotive lights are better than they've ever been, but there's a trade-off.

zh.title: 汽车前灯如何变得更亮、更白和更刺眼
zh.summary: 现代汽车前灯比以往任何时候都更亮、技术更先进，但亮度和色温的提高伴随而来的是眩光增加，可能会使其他司机致盲。

title: A Marc Benioff-backed startup thinks AI can solve the AI deployment problem
summary: Marc Benioff-backed startup June emerged from stealth with $20 million in pre-seed funding to simplify AI deployment and adoption challenges for organizations.
content: June emerged from stealth today with a $20 million pre-seed round to make AI adoption simpler.

zh.title: 一家得到Marc Benioff支持的初创公司认为AI可以解决AI部署问题
zh.summary: 得到Marc Benioff支持的初创公司June从隐形模式中推出，获得了2000万美元的种子前融资，旨在为组织简化AI部署和应用挑战。
